script.title: Why a Doctor Had a Pump's Handle Removed

lines: Parish leaders pulled the handle off a London pump because one doctor asked.
In three days, 127 people near Broad Street died of cholera.
Most doctors blamed bad air, a poison smell called miasma.
London's top medical officer called John Snow's germ idea peculiar.
So Snow and Reverend Henry Whitehead questioned the families of the dead.
The deaths circled one pump on Broad Street.
Some families even fetched its water, though other pumps were nearer.
Snow's microscope couldn't prove the water was deadly. But the pattern was clear.
On the evening of September seventh, Snow met the parish leaders.
The next day, the handle came off.
You see, it's like a whole family getting sick after one meal.
You don't blame the air. You check what they all swallowed.
Later, they found the well was dug just three feet from an old cesspit.
Water from washing a sick baby's nappies drained into it.
And the workers at the brewery nearby? Not one caught cholera.
They drank their daily beer, not the pump water.
But when the outbreak faded, officials put the handle back and rejected his theory.
Today, a plaque on that street shows a pump with no handle.

claims.claim: Over three days, 127 people on or near Broad Street died of cholera.
Miasma theory blamed cholera on bad air from decaying matter.
John Simon, London's lead medical officer, called Snow's germ theory peculiar.
Snow, helped by Reverend Henry Whitehead, talked to local residents and traced the outbreak to the Broad Street pump.
Some families sent to the Broad Street pump though other pumps were nearer, because they preferred its water.
Snow's chemical and microscope examination of the water did not conclusively prove its danger; the pattern of deaths persuaded the parish authorities.
Snow met the Board of Guardians of St James's parish on the evening of 7 September, and the handle was removed the next day.
The well was dug 3 feet from an old cesspit, and waste water from washing a sick baby's nappies drained into it.
None of the workers at the nearby brewery caught cholera; they had a daily beer allowance and did not drink the pump water.
After the epidemic subsided, officials replaced the pump handle and rejected Snow's theory.
A plaque where the pump stood shows a water pump with its handle removed.

cast.snow: a 41 year old English doctor with short dark wavy hair, a clean shaven narrow face, thin lips, deep-set grey eyes, a black frock coat, a grey waistcoat, a white high collar and a black necktie, 1850s
cast.whitehead: a 28 year old English vicar with fair curly hair, a round friendly face, rosy cheeks, a black clerical coat and a white clerical collar, 1850s
cast.simon: a 38 year old London health official with a neat full black beard, a high bald forehead, a brown overcoat with a fur collar and a grey top hat, 1850s
cast.mother: a 30 year old poor London woman with red hair tied under a white cotton cap, a faded blue cotton dress and a brown wool shawl, 1850s
cast.brewer: a burly 50 year old brewery worker with a thick ginger beard, a flat cloth cap, rolled-up shirt sleeves and a grey canvas apron, 1850s
